doc.title: John Beal interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 18, 2024

title: The bass and amplification
summary: The bass has not changed despite technology; Beal owns a 280-year-old bass and prefers playing acoustic without an amp, using a mic when needed.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique

blocks.x: It’s a good feeling isn’t it, but when I said why did he say that about the bass, do you think the bass is — this was a question for later but I’m going to try it now. Music has changed the way it’s produced so much over the years, and I’m wondering if the bass has been somewhat immune from all the changes in technology?

Well it’s been affected by pick-ups and, you know the high-tech method of recording to a certain extent. I was just listening to a couple of Chet Baker records recorded in Italy with these bizarre mixes and it sounded like they were just recording the bass through a pick-up that sounded like a banjo you know. But the bass has not changed. I have a bass that’s 280 years old, one of my basses, and it’s got the same — the sound improves year by year by aging. And a contractor called me up recently about a show that they were doing, “Jelly’s Last Jam” and they were very — the director was very interested in having period piano, period drums, and the contractor asked me is there such a thing as a period bass. I said no, they’re the same. I mean all basses are a little different because there’s no set model but a bass is a bass you know. You look at a modern bass and it looks like an old bass, the same shape except maybe the varnish is showing less wear.

When you came up here in 2005 to play with Kenny — and I recall that you didn’t want an amplifier, the room was acoustically really wonderful, but do you find that your fellow musicians on a club date or something play differently volume-wise when you don’t have an amplifier? Are they sympathetic to your bass set-up?

It’s a great question because I believe that the bass really affects the balance of a band or an orchestra. And one reason I got away from amplifying was because if you use a pick- up and you bow it sounds like a baritone sax you know. So you have to get a full tone with no amp. And you get the real sound of the bass. But sometimes you have to use the

microphone because of the venue or the size of the orchestra. You know the size of the hall you’re playing in, the theater. But I really got away from amplified acoustic bass. I went through a whole period where I used a pick-up. Because doing TV shows and live shows, it’s just practically necessary if they want to hear the notes you know, because you’re not separated acoustically from drums and all the other louder instruments.
